Abstract

Gradient-based design needs the derivative of an objective with respect to the parameters a designer edits, such as a hole radius or a fillet radius. In a boundary-representation (BRep) kernel those parameters pass through Boolean operations, filleting and tessellation, which make discrete choices. We freeze the tessellation’s topology at the current parameters and differentiate its node positions: surface nodes by evaluating the kernel’s analytic surfaces on dual numbers, vertices and trim curves by implicit differentiation of the surface equations, with tangency rows for fillet blends. The result is exact for the frozen mesh, extends to directional second derivatives and to a transposed (reverse) pass, and feeds mass properties and a rigid-body adjoint with penalty contact. A change of topology is reported as an error.

We validate against finite differences of fresh rebuilds that share no tessellation with the seam, and state where the method falls short: the derivative of the frozen mesh differs from the continuum by the polygonization error (6.7% for a fillet at 16 segments per circle, 0.11% at 128), a plan stays valid for parameter steps up to mm, and the finite-difference checks found two errors in the seam on filleted, drilled parts, which we describe and have fixed.

1 Introduction

A mechanical designer works in parameters: the depth of a pocket, the radius of a bore, the radius of a fillet. An optimizer that serves that designer needs , the derivative of an objective (a mass, an inertia, the outcome of a simulation) with respect to those parameters. Between and anything measurable sit Boolean operations, fillet construction and tessellation, each of which makes discrete decisions: which faces survive a Boolean, in which order they are sewn, how many segments approximate a circle. Mainstream commercial kernels expose no parameter derivatives, so users fall back on finite differences of full rebuilds, at two rebuilds per parameter.

This is not a new problem, and our approach is not new in outline. Engineering Sketch Pad computes tessellation sensitivities on a parametric BRep: the motion of every grid point with respect to every design parameter, on a tessellation whose topology is kept consistent between the base and perturbed models, with sensitivities found on Nodes, then Edges, then Faces 1,2. Those sensitivities are analytic for most construction operations and fall back to finite differences for others, filleting among them 1. Banović et al. differentiate the Open CASCADE kernel itself by operator overloading 3,4.

We describe the same idea, which we call the seam, in vcad, our open-source Rust BRep kernel, and extend it in four directions:

  • Fillets analytically. A fillet radius moves every blend’s radius and axis at once, and its blends meet their support faces tangentially, which makes the implicit system at their corner vertices rank-deficient. We add tangency rows that complete it (Section 3.3), so one fillet parameter, moving 20 surfaces, is differentiated without finite differences.
  • Second order. Directional second derivatives of mass properties, with the node accelerations of cones and tori (Section 4).
  • A transposed pass. Node velocities are linear in per-surface seed values; transposing those maps gives the derivative for every parameter from one pass (Section 5).
  • Rigid-body dynamics. Mass-property and contact cotangents from a discrete trajectory adjoint pulled back through the seam (Section 7).

We validate every derivative against central finite differences of rebuilds tessellated from scratch, which share nothing with the seam’s code (Section 8), and describe the two cases where the checks found errors in the seam. A script regenerates every number in this paper from a fresh clone (Section 10).

1.1 Scope and limits

  • The derivative is that of the frozen mesh. The seam differentiates the mesh the kernel produces at , with segment counts and triangulation held fixed. It differs from the continuum shape derivative by the polygonization error, which falls as in the number of segments: for a filleted cube at 16 segments per full circle (four per quarter-blend) the fillet-radius derivative is 6.7% larger in magnitude than the continuum one, and 0.11% at 128 (Figure 8).
  • A plan is valid only near where it was captured. Re-evaluating a plan matches every node to its capture-time position within mm. On the five-parameter box of Section 8.4, every parameter can move by mm before that match fails. The optimizer therefore captures a fresh plan at every iterate.
  • Segment counts can change between iterates. vcad’s Boolean rims are sag-adaptive: their arc count depends on the radius. Sweeping the box’s hole radius from 1.6 to 2.4 mm changes the node count 20 times, and each change moves the volume by up to of its value. Across iterates is therefore piecewise smooth with small jumps. The optimizer does not reject a step because its node count differs from the last iterate’s, because each iterate’s gradient is taken on its own plan; the jumps show up as noise in the line search.
  • No derivatives across topology changes. When a perturbation would change the topology (a blind hole breaking through, a fillet consuming a face), the seam detects it with a topology signature and per-node correspondence checks and returns an error, and the optimizer shrinks the step (Figure 1).
  • Seedings synthesized from the build function are not exact. They are central differences of surface fields, accurate to , and they cost two rebuilds per parameter (Section 6).
  • Contact is phyz’s differentiable penalty model, a per-vertex spring–damper against a ground plane without friction, not a GJK/EPA collision pipeline 5. The trajectory adjoint supports single-degree-of-freedom joints, open-loop control and objectives on the final state only.
  • Everything runs on CPU in double precision.

2 Background and related work

Parametric CAD sensitivities. Structural shape optimization has long used design velocities, the sensitivity of boundary points to design variables 6,7. For CAD models these come from three routes. Finite differences of rebuilds with point correspondence are the most general and the most expensive; Robinson et al. and Agarwal et al. compute parametric design velocities this way for use with adjoint solvers 8,9. Differentiating the kernel by operator overloading gives exact derivatives of the kernel’s operations: Banović et al. and Mykhaskiv et al. differentiate Open CASCADE and couple it to a discrete adjoint CFD solver 3,4, and Xu et al. differentiate a NURBS-based design chain 10. Engineering Sketch Pad differentiates its own constructive solid geometry process analytically where it can and uses finite differences elsewhere, and maps the result onto a consistent tessellation 1,2. Our seam is closest to Engineering Sketch Pad: we leave the kernel’s combinatorial code undifferentiated and differentiate the map from parameters to a tessellation of fixed topology. What we add is the analytic treatment of fillets, second derivatives, a transposed pass, and the coupling to rigid-body dynamics with contact. Isogeometric analysis avoids the tessellation by computing on the CAD basis 11.

Differentiable CAD programs. Cascaval et al. write CAD programs in an automatically differentiable language for bidirectional editing, and do not optimize across changes of topology 12. Michel and Boubekeur compute parameter updates for direct manipulation of procedural shapes 13. Schulz et al. precompute a design space of CAD parameters for interactive optimization 14.

Differentiable rendering and other representations. Differentiable rasterizers 15,16 and path tracers 17 compute derivatives of images with respect to the vertices of a mesh of fixed connectivity, as ours is. Worchel and Alexa extract a mesh from parametric curves and surfaces for a differentiable mesh renderer and report that naive differentiable tessellation is fragile 18. Signed distance fields, learned 19 or analytic, are differentiable almost everywhere and can be rendered differentiably 20, and program synthesis recovers CSG trees from shapes 21,22. These representations give up the BRep’s exact faces, trims and fillets.

Differentiable physics and co-design. Differentiable simulators include rigid-body formulations with contact 23–25 and differentiable programming systems 26. Robot co-design work optimizes morphology and control jointly 27,28, usually over parametric primitives rather than CAD models. Placing a solver or a simulation inside a differentiable program as one step with a known adjoint is standard 29; our rollout coupling is such a step written by hand.

3 The differentiable seam

3.1 Frozen plans

vcad represents solids as BReps whose faces carry analytic surfaces (plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, torus, bilinear patch, B-spline), with Boolean operations, filleting and a tessellator. Two properties of the kernel shaped the design. First, its Boolean and fillet code is order-nondeterministic: two builds of the same model can enumerate isomorphic topology in different orders, flip a blend cylinder’s axis or rotate its reference direction, so traversal order cannot carry node identity from one build to another. Second, the stock mesh stores 32-bit positions, at which a central difference with is meaningless, so the seam emits its own 64-bit mesh.

Capturing a plan tessellates once at and classifies every node:

  • Vertex nodes coincide with a topology vertex. Their velocity comes from implicit differentiation (Section 3.3).
  • Surface nodes are interior to a face, stored as fixed surface coordinates . Their position is for the surface’s fields (offset, radius, axis, half-angle).
  • Trim nodes lie on the intersection of two faces with independent normals but are not topology vertices, for example a ring on a cylinder’s cap. Their position is the Newton solution of , with the intersection tangent, so a trim node follows the moving trim whichever surface carries .

A plan carries a topology signature (a sorted multiset of per-face descriptors, invariant to isomorphic reordering) and each node’s capture-time position. Re-evaluating at a nearby resolves vertices and faces geometrically, by nearest match after transporting the stored through the rebuilt surface’s frame. If any node lands more than mm from where it should, evaluation fails with a lost-correspondence error; if the signature changes, it fails with a topology error.

3.2 Surface nodes

Every analytic surface in vcad is generic over a scalar type, so it can be evaluated on dual numbers with 30. A parameter is connected to the surfaces it moves by a seeding: a map from surface index to field velocities (translate by , grow the radius at rate , open the cone at rate ). Seeds on one surface add, which is what a fillet needs: when the fillet radius grows, each blend cylinder’s radius grows at rate 1 while its axis retreats from the edge, and each corner sphere does the same in three coordinates. For a surface node, the dual part of is .

3.3 Vertices and trims

A topology vertex lies on every surface incident to it. Each incident surface has an implicit form : for a plane , a cylinder , a sphere , and for a cone with apex , axis and half-angle ,

Differentiating gives one linear row per surface,

We solve the rows by Gram–Schmidt, carrying the right-hand side. Independent rows fix components of , dependent rows must agree within tolerance (otherwise the solve fails), and directions no row constrains stay at zero, so a node on a circular rim keeps its angular parameter. Three planes at a box corner give a full solve; a plane and a cylinder at a hole rim give a rank-2 solve with a frozen tangent.

Two refinements were needed. Boolean sewing does not always pair the half-edges around a rim, so topological adjacency under-constrains some vertices, and the seam also collects rows by geometric incidence. And a fillet blend touches its support face tangentially, so the blend’s row is parallel to the plane’s and the system is rank-deficient exactly where the corner vertex slides along the face. The vertex must stay on the tangent curve; for a cylinder of axis tangent to a plane of normal we add the row with , and two such rows for a sphere. With these rows the corner vertex of a filleted cube at moves at per unit radius, as the closed form requires.

4 Quantities of interest

4.1 Mass properties

Volume, mass, centroid and inertia tensor follow from signed-tetrahedron integrals over the closed mesh 31. The integrals are written once over a generic scalar, so evaluating them at dual-number node positions gives every quantity and its derivative along in one pass. A downstream functional enters through the contraction

with known in closed form from the divergence theorem.

4.2 Second order

For one direction in parameter space,

Evaluating the volume integral on nested duals carries both terms; the work is in the node accelerations . A surface node on a plane, cylinder or sphere is linear in its fields, so its acceleration is the first-order lift fed the field accelerations. Cone and torus points are not linear in their fields (, the two torus radii), so their surface nodes are lifted on nested duals. Vertex and trim nodes solve the implicit system differentiated twice,

with the same row gradients as the first-order solve; cones and tori contribute closed-form curvature terms because their is not constant. For least-squares objectives we also form the Gauss–Newton Hessian , which drops the residual-curvature term and is exact at zero residual.

5 The transposed pass and optimization

A seeding assigns to each surface a vector of seed values: a translation in and one rate per scalar field of that surface’s kind. Each node’s velocity is linear in the seed values of the surfaces that determine it: , where is the Jacobian of node ‘s recipe with respect to surface ‘s fields at the frozen plan. The transposed pass contracts the transposes with :

One pass computes every per-surface cotangent ; each parameter then costs a few dot products. No tape is recorded. The transposed vertex solve runs the same Gram–Schmidt elimination, carrying each coefficient as a linear functional of the rows, and each row’s dependence on its seeds is read off by calling the forward row constructor with unit seeds. Forward and transposed passes therefore share the rows: their agreement checks the linear algebra, not the rows.

The optimizer is L-BFGS with memory 8 32, box projection and an Armijo line search on the projected step. Each iterate rebuilds the part and captures a fresh plan. A trial step that fails with a topology or correspondence error counts as a failed step. A curvature pair is dropped when or when its line search had to shrink past such an error, and a direction that is not a descent direction clears the memory.

6 Seeding synthesis and documents

Writing a seeding by hand is error-prone on real parts. Synthesis derives it from the build function: it rebuilds at , matches each base surface to its counterparts by frame-invariant geometric identity (a plane by its normal up to sign and its offset, a cylinder by its axis line and radius, a sphere by center and radius), and reads field velocities off central differences of the matched fields. Surface fields have no combinatorial structure, so the difference is accurate to , but the seeding, and every gradient computed with it, carries that error. It also costs two rebuilds per parameter: on the five-parameter box, synthesizing all five seedings takes 917 ms, slightly more than a finite-difference gradient of the whole objective (860 ms). Synthesis pays off only when a seeding is reused across many evaluations at one ; deriving seedings symbolically from the feature tree would remove both costs and is not implemented.

A named parameter of a .vcad document is differentiated the same way: the parameter is bound, the document is evaluated to one BRep per part, the seeding is synthesized, and each solid part returns . Evaluations at must produce the same number of parts, or the call fails.

7 Gradients through rigid-body rollouts

In a rollout of an articulated rigid-body system without contact, the geometry of body enters the dynamics only through its ten mass-property scalars . With contact, it also enters through the positions of the vertices that touch. The chain rule is

comes from a discrete adjoint over semi-implicit Euler in the phyz simulator, written over Featherstone’s articulated-body algorithm 33; its within-step Jacobian columns are evaluated on dual numbers, one lane per column. is the seam’s mass-property derivative. For contact, phyz applies a penalty force at every vertex of the body’s frozen-plan mesh that lies below the ground, its adjoint returns on those vertices, and the transposed pass turns that into . A rollout the adjoint cannot express (state feedback, multi-DOF joints) falls back to central differences on the ten scalars, which needs about twenty re-simulations per body and no CAD rebuild.

8 Results

All results come from vcad’s test suite at commit 7af5dce81b and from the experiments in repro/ (Section 10), run in the release profile on one thread of a 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-12900K (rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18)). Each test asserts a tolerance, for most first-order checks; the values below are what the tests measured. We use two finite-difference references. Same-plan FD rebuilds the part at and re-evaluates the frozen plan captured at ; it checks the seam’s derivative of its own plan evaluator. Rebuild FD tessellates each rebuild from scratch and shares no code with the seam beyond the kernel itself; it is the independent check, but it is noisy at small , where node placements differ between rebuilds, and it carries truncation error at large . Relative errors are taken against the larger magnitude.

8.1 Validation against finite differences

The models are: an extruded mm rectangle, depth mm; a mm box minus a through-hole of radius mm (32 circle segments, whose sag-adaptive rim has 112); a cylinder of radius 5 mm and height 8 mm (24 segments); a 10 mm cube with every edge filleted at mm (16 segments per full circle, 836 nodes); a cone frustum with base radius 5, top radius 3 and height 8 mm (apex at 20 mm, 24 segments), parameterized by half-angle and by height; and a torus with , mm (24 segments).

Every model passes both checks, and the rebuild FD, which is independent of the seam, confirms the same-plan results to the accuracy its noise and truncation allow. Where a discrete closed form exists the seam meets it to rounding: the hole’s mesh cross-section is the inscribed 112-gon, so , met to the cone’s half-angle derivative meets the prismatoid volume with to the cylinder-height derivative meets the N-gon cap area to and the extrusion’s is exactly the cross-section area. The mass-property derivatives behave the same way: of the extrusion meets its closed form to , and the cylinder’s inertia derivative with respect to radius meets same-plan FD to .

8.2 The polygonization gap

The seam’s derivative is that of the mesh, so it differs from the continuum derivative by the polygonization error. For the hole that error is the factor with , at 112 segments. For the filleted cube it is larger, and larger in magnitude than the continuum value, because an inscribed polygon removes more material than the circular blend and removes it faster as grows. At 16 segments per full circle (four per quarter-blend) the seam’s against the continuum −68.217, a gap of 6.7%; the gap falls as (Figure 8). Mass properties at four segments per quarter-blend are a coarse model of a filleted part, and the remedy is resolution, not a different derivative.

8.3 Transposed pass, synthesis and second order

For the torus the rebuild difference of converges onto the seam’s second derivative as grows (from at to at ); the in vcad’s own test is its smaller step. The filleted cube behaves the same way: the difference reaches −40.7642 at against the seam’s −40.7643, and a five-point stencil on one frozen plan agrees with the seam to . An earlier revision of the kernel failed this check by at every step (Section 8.4).

8.4 Five parameters of a filleted, drilled box

The part is a box of dimensions with every edge filleted at radius and a centered through-hole of radius : 6 planes, 12 blend cylinders, 8 corner spheres and the hole wall, 1046 mesh nodes at (16 segments per circle). The objective is the squared relative miss of five quantities (volume, the three centroid coordinates and ) against their values at mm, starting from mm. The five-by-five Jacobian of the quantities has determinant 35689 and smallest pivot 0.34, so the parameters are locally identifiable.

Two errors the finite differences caught. At , same-plan FD at agrees with the seam’s gradient to for , for , for the fillet radius and for the hole radius, and rebuild FD of the fillet-radius component reaches at (Figure 7). This was not so in the kernel revision we first measured (d10f279). There the fillet-radius component sat from same-plan FD and the component , at every step from to , and the filleted cube’s second derivative missed by . An error that does not move with the step is not finite-difference noise, and both had causes in the seam. A Boolean rounds the centers of a corner sphere and its blend cylinder through single precision, so the two surfaces cross at about rad instead of meeting tangentially; the tessellator classified their shared arc as a trim between two surfaces and tracked it with an ill-conditioned Newton solve. Such near-tangent pairs now take the sphere’s surface rule, which removed the fillet-radius and second-derivative errors. Separately, a vertex on the hole’s rim has only plane and cylinder rows, which left its slide along the rim at zero while the kernel moves it with the hole; volume cannot see that, moments can. Those directions now ride with the vertex’s curved surface. Both fixes are in the pinned commit, each with a regression test.

What exact derivatives buy here is not only that L-BFGS converges: with rebuild FD at a well-chosen step () it reaches in a similar number of iterations and stalls at mm in this run (an earlier run of the same driver reached ; rebuild FD is not repeatable to that level, because rebuilds do not place nodes identically). They buy cost and robustness. A seam gradient (rebuild, capture, one pass and one transposed pass) takes 85 ms on this part against 860 ms for a rebuild-FD gradient, a factor of 10 at five parameters that grows with the parameter count; and FD at a too-small () or too-large () step ends and mm from . Because the residuals are square and vanish at , Gauss–Newton with the exact Jacobian is the natural method, and Levenberg–Marquardt reaches in 4 iterations and 0.62 s.

The rebuild dominates each iterate: 82 ms against 0.9 ms for the capture, 0.24 ms for one forward pass, 0.05 ms for the dual mass properties of that pass, and 0.44 ms for the transposed pass. The transposed pass costs about 1.8 forward passes on this part, so it pays from two parameters up. (On the filleted cube without the hole, Figure 12, it costs about three, because that part has fewer vertex rows to transpose relative to its surface nodes.)

8.5 A fillet radius and a flywheel

Projected gradient descent on the fillet radius of the 10 mm cube alone recovers the radius whose volume matches a target, mm from mm, landing at 2.2 mm in 12 accepted iterates.

Each flywheel iterate takes seconds because the build does: five Booleans at 24 segments take 4.2 s, against 7 ms to capture its 2552-node plan.

8.6 A named document parameter

A .vcad document whose cylinder radius is bound to the named parameter r differentiates with no hand seeding: 501.848 against the N-gon closed form 501.848 (), and agrees with FD of document rebuilds to . A document written in vcad’s loon language and one whose parameter is declared with defparam reach the same closed form to and . These gradients use synthesized seedings and carry their error.

8.7 Shape through dynamics and contact

The cylinder rows are a check of the chain on a body whose mass properties have closed forms. The last row exercises the seam through dynamics: a 20 mm cube with every edge filleted at 2 mm rests on one blended edge, held by a vertical prismatic joint, and is its settled height. The fillet radius moves 20 surfaces. Growing it raises the lowest point of the blend by per unit radius, so the surface channel alone would give m per mm; the gradient, , adds the mass channel and the change in which blend vertices touch, and matches a rebuild-and-resimulate FD to .

8.8 Pixels to CAD parameters

The transposed pass accepts any cotangent on the plan’s nodes, including one from a renderer. With the irys differentiable path tracer 34 we pulled an image gradient back to a CAD dimension on a real part: the left shoulder-pitch output plate of the rose robot arm, a 3 mm rounded plate with a 49 mm bearing bore and twelve 4.4 mm bolt holes. θ is the bore diameter; the plan has 4942 nodes at 32 circle segments and a synthesized seeding. irys renders the plan’s mesh as it is against an empty background at 160 × 128 pixels, so the whole derivative comes from visibility edges, and its edge sampler returns on every node for a fixed smooth image loss ( samples, 8 seeds).

A rebuild FD is not possible here. A rebuild at loses correspondence for mm and changes topology at 0.05 mm, where the bore rim’s sag-adaptive arc count drops by two vertices, while at mm the render FD is dominated by quadrature noise. The last row therefore moves the plan’s nodes along their same-plan FD velocities instead of rebuilding, which checks the renderer’s derivative but not the seam’s; the seam’s part of the chain is checked by the third row.

8.9 Cost

9 Discussion

Why freeze the tessellation. Differentiating the kernel’s code has to give some answer at every branch: which face a Boolean keeps, how a fillet orders its blends, how many segments a circle gets. Those answers are piecewise constant in , and in vcad they are also order-nondeterministic. Freezing the plan makes the discrete state explicit and checkable. The cost is the limits of Section 1.1: a plan is valid for steps of mm on the five-parameter box, segment counts change between iterates, and the derivative is that of the mesh. For optimization this has been enough on every part we tried, because each iterate captures a new plan and the jumps between plans are of order of the objective; for an objective that depends on fine surface detail, the polygonization gap would dominate before the jumps do.

What the finite differences show. On every plane, cylinder, cone and torus model, same-plan FD, rebuild FD and the seam agree. On filleted solids rebuild FD is noisy at small steps, because rebuilds place nodes differently, and has to be read at a step of to mm (Figure 7). At those steps it confirms the seam on the filleted cube and the filleted, drilled box. Same-plan FD is the sharper test, since it has no rebuild noise, and it is the one that exposed the two seam errors of Section 8.4: each showed as an error that stayed fixed while the step moved over two decades.

Toward an operator graph. The rollout coupling of Section 7 composes three steps by hand: the seam (parameters to node positions, with its transposed pass), mass properties (node positions to ten scalars per body) and the phyz adjoint (scalars and contact vertices to ). Each is a step with a forward map and an exact vector–Jacobian product, which is the shape of an operator node in a differentiable program 29. We are building that graph on the tang tensor compiler 35, where linear solves and simulations become nodes with their own adjoints; none of that is evaluated here.

Remaining gaps. Cone-tangent-to-plane tangency rows are not implemented; fillets with asymmetric corners or three blends at a vertex fall back to an older pipeline that is not differentiated; the contact model is frictionless; and the method is demonstrated only on vcad. Nothing in it depends on vcad beyond analytic surfaces that evaluate on dual numbers and a tessellator that can classify its nodes.

10 Reproducibility

repro/repro.sh clones vcad at 7af5dce81bea4aea801dd37128b912ab3a3c6cd2 (its lockfile pins phyz, loon and tang) and applies report.patch, which adds eprintln! lines after statements in vcad’s tests that already compute a measured quantity, so each test still asserts its own tolerance and prints the value it checks. It then copies in paper_experiments.rs and paper_contact_fillet.rs, the experiments added for this paper (rebuild FD, step sweeps, resolution study, optimizer baselines, costs, plan radius, segment-count jumps, second-order sweeps, the flywheel L-BFGS run and the filleted-box contact rollout), runs everything, runs irys.sh for the rose-arm benchmark, and writes data/measured.tsv. This document reads every measured number, table cell and plotted point from that file. The run used for this draft took place on 2026-11-10T16:01Z on Linux 6.8.0-147-generic x86_64.

11 Conclusion

Freezing a BRep’s tessellation and differentiating its node positions gives derivatives of CAD parameters, fillet radii included, that are exact for the mesh, extend to second order and a transposed pass, and carry through to mass properties and rigid-body dynamics with contact. The approach follows Engineering Sketch Pad’s tessellation sensitivities; our additions are analytic fillets, second derivatives, the transposed pass and the dynamics coupling. Its limits are those of the frozen mesh, a polygonization gap that falls as and plans valid for small steps. Checking against finite differences on one frozen plan found two errors in the seam, both since fixed. vcad, the experiments and the data are open source.
